opus-5.5.text:
That's a great question, and it's one I get a lot. The short answer is that removal-based methods are grounded in a very clear and intuitive principle: if you want to know how much a feature matters, you see what happens to the model's prediction when that feature's information is taken away. That's a simple idea, but it's surprisingly powerful, and it connects to a long tradition of thinking in cooperative game theory, sensitivity analysis, and even causal reasoning.

When my group and colleagues started looking across the landscape of explanation methods, we saw that many of them, like LIME, SHAP, permutation importance, occlusion, and others, could be understood within a single framework. They all remove features, they differ in how they remove them, what model behavior they look at, and how they summarize the results. Once you see that, you can reason much more carefully about which choices are well-justified. And the Shapley value comes out of that analysis as a principled way of summarizing, because it satisfies properties like efficiency, symmetry, and consistency that people care about when they want to trust an attribution.

Gradient-based methods are certainly faster, and they have their place, especially for very high-dimensional inputs like images. But gradients measure local sensitivity, which isn't always the same as importance. A feature can matter a lot to a prediction and still have a small gradient at that point, for example because of saturation. Removal-based methods ask a more directly meaningful question.

As for the computational cost, I see it as an engineering challenge rather than a fundamental flaw. We've put a lot of effort into making these methods practical: model-specific algorithms like TreeSHAP, which computes exact Shapley values for tree ensembles in polynomial time; better sampling and regression-based estimators; and amortized approaches where you train a separate model to output explanations in a single forward pass. With those advances, the cost has come down dramatically.

And honestly, in the settings I care most about, like biomedicine and clinical decision-making, getting the explanation right matters much more than shaving off computation time. If a clinician or a biologist is going to act on an explanation, or if we're using explanations to audit a model for shortcuts or bias, I'd rather pay a bit more compute for something with solid theoretical footing.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks, it's great to be here. So I think the honest answer is that removal-based approaches, and SHAP in particular, are the only family of methods where I actually know what the explanation means.

When we were developing SHAP, the starting point wasn't "let's make this fast." The starting point was: if I give you a number that says feature X contributed this much to this prediction, what does that number represent? And with a lot of the gradient-based or attention-based methods, the honest answer is, well, it's the derivative at a point, or it's whatever the attention weights happen to be, and there's no clear contract between that number and the behavior of the model. Removal-based methods have a very clean contract. You ask: what happens to the model's output when this feature is absent? And the Shapley value just gives you a principled way to average over all the different contexts in which a feature could be absent, so that the credit is assigned fairly and the attributions actually sum up to the prediction.

That axiomatic grounding matters enormously in the settings I care about. A lot of my work is in biomedicine, in clinical settings, in genomics. If a model says a patient is at high risk and a clinician is going to act on that, I can't hand them an explanation that's essentially a heuristic. I need to be able to say, this attribution satisfies properties like efficiency and symmetry, and if two features play identical roles they get identical credit, and if the model doesn't use a feature at all it gets zero. Those are things a domain expert can reason about, and they're also things that let us use the explanations downstream, for feature selection, for auditing, for discovering biology.

Now, on the computational cost, I'd push back a little on how big of a barrier that really is in practice. The exponential cost is the naive case. For tree models we have TreeSHAP, which is exact and polynomial. For deep models there's a whole line of work on amortized explanation, where you train a separate model to produce the explanations, so you pay the cost once up front and then explaining a new instance is a single forward pass. And there's been a lot of progress on better estimators, on understanding how feature removal should be done, whether you marginalize or condition, and how those choices affect what you get. So the cost has come down a lot, and the parts of it that remain I'm often willing to pay, because the alternative is a cheap explanation that I can't trust.

I'd also say that in the applications we've worked on, computation is rarely the actual bottleneck. The bottleneck is whether anyone believes the explanation and whether it leads to a decision or an insight. If an explanation is wrong or ambiguous, it doesn't matter how fast it was. So I'd rather spend the compute and get something with a well-defined meaning than save it and end up with something that looks like an explanation but doesn't really commit to anything.

astra-6.text:
For me, the appeal is that removal-based approaches ask a very concrete question: How does the model’s prediction change when a particular piece of information is unavailable? That gives us a way to understand what the model relies on, rather than just looking at its parameters or how it responds to a tiny perturbation.

The challenge is that features work together. A feature may be important in one context and less important in another. SHAP provides a principled way to account for that by considering a feature’s contribution across different subsets of the other features. That is computationally demanding, but the underlying question is meaningful.

Of course, we have to be careful about what “removing” information means, especially when features are correlated. These explanations describe the model’s behavior; they don’t automatically establish causality. But I would rather start with a well-defined question and find ways to compute or approximate the answer efficiently than choose an explanation simply because it is cheap.

For me, the appeal is that removal-based methods ask a very concrete question: How does the model’s prediction change when a particular piece of information is unavailable? That gives us a way to probe what the model relies on, rather than simply looking at its parameters.

SHAP takes that idea further by considering a feature’s contribution across different combinations of available features. That matters because a feature’s contribution can depend on what other information the model has. The computation can be expensive, but I think having a principled definition of what we’re trying to explain is valuable. We can then work on approximating that quantity more efficiently.

Of course, we have to be careful about what “removing” a feature means, especially when features are correlated. A SHAP value explains model behavior under those assumptions; it doesn’t automatically establish a causal relationship.
